lead: A real aircraft part rarely sees a steady stress: a gust, a landing or a pressurisation cycle pushes it up and down. Every fluctuating stress splits into a steady mean part and a to-and-fro alternating part. Two ratios fix the shape of the cycle. A constant-life diagram then folds both parts into a single factor of safety against fatigue. Only a few universities teach this topic at this depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.8 for the endurance limit and the S-N curve, and Chapter 3.6 for combining stresses at a point.

blocks.text: One fatigue cycle runs between a maximum stress σ_max and a minimum stress σ_min, both in MPa, tension positive. Split it about its midpoint.

blocks.where: σ_m is the mean stress, the steady part (MPa); σ_a is the alternating stress, the half-swing about the mean (MPa); the range is σ_r = σ_max − σ_min = 2σ_a.

blocks.text: Two ratios fix the shape of the cycle. The stress ratio is R = σ_min/σ_max. The amplitude ratio is A = σ_a/σ_m. The value of R tells you which cycle you have.

items: R = −1: fully reversed, σ_m = 0 and σ_max = −σ_min — the rotating-bending test of Chapter 3.8.
R = 0: zero to maximum (pulsating tension), σ_min = 0, so σ_m = σ_a = σ_max/2.
R = 1: steady load, σ_a = 0; fatigue does not arise.

blocks.text: Plot σ_m across and σ_a up. Each point is one cycle. For a chosen life a curve separates safe cycles from failing ones. It meets the vertical axis at the endurance limit S_e, where σ_m = 0, and the horizontal axis at a static strength, where σ_a = 0.
Goodman: σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_u = 1;  Gerber: σ_a/S_e + (σ_m/S_u)² = 1;  Soderberg: σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_y = 1
blocks.where: S_e is the endurance limit (MPa), S_u the ultimate tensile strength (MPa), S_y the yield strength (MPa).

blocks.text: Goodman is a straight line from S_e to S_u and the usual conservative choice. Gerber is a parabola through the same two points and follows ductile test data better. Soderberg runs from S_e to S_y and is the most conservative. The Langer line σ_a + σ_m = S_y is plain first-cycle yielding: when the peak stress σ_max = σ_a + σ_m reaches S_y, the part yields at once, whatever its fatigue life.

The factor of safety n scales both stresses until the load point touches the curve. Put nσ_m and nσ_a into the line: Goodman gives 1/n = σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_u, Soderberg gives 1/n = σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_y. Gerber gives a quadratic in n; take the positive root.

figure.caption: Constant-life lines for S_e = 400 MPa, S_u = 800 MPa, S_y = 600 MPa. The load point (100, 200) MPa lies inside all three, so the part is safe. Goodman, the straight line to 800 MPa, is the usual design line.

spec.aria: Three constant-life lines falling from an alternating stress of 400 MPa to zero, Soderberg the steepest, Gerber the outermost, with the worked load point at a mean of 100 MPa and an alternating stress of 200 MPa.

examples.question: A steel aircraft fitting sees σ_max = 300 MPa and σ_min = −100 MPa. Take S_e = 400 MPa, S_u = 800 MPa and S_y = 600 MPa. Find σ_m, σ_a, R and A, the factor of safety by Goodman, Soderberg and Gerber, and check first-cycle yielding.
steps: Yield check: σ_a + σ_m = 200 + 100 = 300 MPa, below S_y = 600 MPa, so the first cycle does not yield.
examples.answer: σ_m = 100 MPa, σ_a = 200 MPa, R = −0.33, A = 2.0; n = 1.60 by Goodman, 1.50 by Soderberg and 1.89 by Gerber, and the fitting does not yield on the first cycle.
examples.check:
smax, smin = 300.0, -100.0
Se, Su, Sy = 400.0, 800.0, 600.0
sm = (smax + smin)/2
sa = (smax - smin)/2
R = smin/smax
A = sa/sm
n_good = 1/(sa/Se + sm/Su)
n_sod = 1/(sa/Se + sm/Sy)
a = (sm/Su)**2
b = sa/Se
n_ger = (-b + (b*b + 4*a)**0.5)/(2*a)
for v in (sm, sa, R, A, n_good, n_sod, n_ger):
    print(round(v, 2))

traps: Dividing S_e by σ_a while a tensile mean stress acts. The mean part also spends life; use σ_a/S_e + σ_m/S_u. The shortcut n = S_e/σ_a holds only at R = −1.
Writing R = σ_max/σ_min. It is R = σ_min/σ_max, and compression keeps its sign: −100/300 = −0.33, not +0.33.
Putting S_u where S_y belongs. The Goodman line ends at S_u, Soderberg at S_y, and the Langer line sits at S_y.
Checking the fatigue line only. A large mean stress yields the part on cycle one, so always test σ_a + σ_m against S_y.

quiz.q: Define σ_m and σ_a in terms of σ_max and σ_min.
quiz.a: σ_m = (σ_max + σ_min)/2, the steady part; σ_a = (σ_max − σ_min)/2, the half-swing about the mean.

quiz.q: Give the stress ratio R for (a) fully reversed, (b) zero to maximum, (c) steady loading.
Why does the Gerber curve sit above the Goodman line between σ_m = 0 and σ_m = S_u?
quiz.a: Both join S_e at σ_m = 0 to S_u at σ_a = 0. Gerber is a concave-down parabola, so at any intermediate mean stress it allows a larger alternating stress than the straight Goodman chord. Goodman is the conservative bound.

quiz.q: A cycle runs from σ_min = 50 MPa to σ_max = 250 MPa. Find σ_m, σ_a, R and A.
S_e = 350 MPa, S_u = 700 MPa, σ_m = 140 MPa, σ_a = 200 MPa. Find n by Goodman and state whether the part is safe.
quiz.a: 1/n = 200/350 + 140/700 = 0.571 + 0.200 = 0.771, so n = 1.30. The point lies inside the line, so it is safe.

quiz.q: A part passes the Goodman check but yields on the first overload. How is that possible?
quiz.a: For ductile steel S_u exceeds S_y, so near the σ_a = 0 end Goodman allows σ_max = σ_a + σ_m above S_y. The fatigue line protects against many cycles, not against first-cycle yield; the Langer line σ_a + σ_m = S_y must be checked as well.

beyond: Not for the exam. A real airframe sees a random load spectrum, not one tidy cycle; rainflow counting breaks the spectrum into blocks and Miner's rule adds up their damage. Damage-tolerance design instead accepts a growing crack and inspects it before it reaches critical length. Search for rainflow counting, Miner's rule and fatigue damage tolerance in aircraft structures.
